chapter_theme: The one song at Rajapuram (ராஜபுரம்) in the Kongu land: the poet lists his own honours as a court poet and asks whether one so gifted should praise base sinners as equal to the legendary patrons; the praise is of Vishnu who saved the elephant.

935.reading: The poet sets out his credentials, conch and crown, golden anklet, whisks and umbrella, palanquin and elephant, many crores of rhythmic languages, mastery of mantra, the four kinds of verse, the title of king of poets, a child Saraswati, the expounder of prabandhas laid down by the Sangam books, and asks whether it is fitting for such a poet to praise some sinners of the five great sins as 'you who equal the ancient one-and-twenty patrons'. The praise tells how the elephant, terrified by the crocodile in the forest pool, cried 'Root!' and Vishnu came on Garuda, names Murugan his nephew, the hero of the Kongu land and lover of the hunter girl, at Rajapuram.
935.nuance: The boast is the argument: the honours (சத்ர, சாமரை, கவிராஜ) are the regalia a court poet earns, and the poet lists them to say they are too good to be spent on பஞ்ச பாதகர். பண்டை மூவெழுவர் are the three sets of seven patrons of Tamil tradition. Whether the poet speaks of himself or in a typical bard's voice is not said.

links.note: Both refuse the bard's flattery of base patrons: 306 mocks calling a miser Pari or Kari, 935 calling sinners the equal of the twenty-one ancient patrons, after listing the poet's own honours.
